Newly hatched neonates of Daphnia mendotae emerge from the brood chamber with a dry weight of 1.41 micrograms , a value that reflects the limited yolk reserves provisioned within the subitaneous egg. Embryonic development proceeds rapidly, and the time from oviposition to the completion of the first instar is strongly temperature-dependent. Experimental rearing at a constant 20 °C [T = 20 °C] reveals a brief duration of 2.6 days [ab = 2.6 days] from birth until the completion of the first instar, a period that encompasses the initial feeding onset and the commencement of filter-feeding on suspended phytoplankton. This short neonatal interval, typical of small-bodied daphniids, is followed immediately by the first juvenile instar, during which the individual undergoes a series of molts before approaching the size threshold associated with reproductive activation.

The transition from the growing juvenile to a reproductively competent adult is marked by the attainment of puberty, which in this species occurs after 4 days since birth [tp = 4 days since birth] when individuals are raised at 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. At this developmental milestone, the individual's dry weight averages 6.094 micrograms , a mass that indicates the completion of the necessary somatic growth before the first clutch can be produced. The first reproduction event, signifying the onset of ovigerous adult life, occurs shortly thereafter. Females then produce successive clutches of parthenogenetic eggs, with each clutch containing 2 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing 2 eggs] during each adult instar. Under optimal thermal conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the frequency of these reproductive events is essentially one clutch per instar [F_R_i = one clutch per instar], reflecting the tight coupling between molting and egg deposition in cladocerans.

While sub-adult and early adult life is characterized by high rates of somatic growth and reproduction, the species eventually reaches a terminal body size. The ultimate dry weight attained by fully grown females is 39.5 micrograms , a mass that represents the asymptotic body size achievable under favorable laboratory conditions. This value is substantially greater than the mass recorded at puberty, underscoring the considerable post-pubertal growth that occurs across the many adult instars. Such continued somatic investment, even after reproductive maturity is reached, is a common life-history strategy among planktonic crustaceans, enabling females to increase clutch volume and offspring size with successive molts as they exploit a seasonally variable resource base.

The total lifespan of Daphnia mendotae under controlled conditions at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] has been documented at 136 days [am = 136 days], a duration that encompasses the entire sequence from the neonate through multiple adult instars to senescence and eventual natural mortality. This relatively extended longevity for a small-bodied cladoceran permits the accumulation of numerous reproductive events across the adult phase. Over the course of this 136-day period (136 days) [am = 136 days], an individual may produce a substantial number of clutches, particularly when maintained at higher temperatures that accelerate development at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The trade-off between longevity and reproduction is mediated by temperature; while higher thermal regimes shorten the total lifespan, they concurrently increase the rate of instar progression and, consequently, the frequency of egg deposition.

Comparisons among congeneric species of Daphnia reveal that the size at puberty and the associated dry weight at birth are consistent with the body-size scaling observed across the genus. In Daphnia mendotae, the dry weight at puberty of 6.094 micrograms  is roughly four times the birth weight of 1.41 micrograms , a proportional increase that is typical of species that reach an ultimate adult size of 39.5 micrograms . The species' reliance on two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch] and one clutch per instar [F_R_i = one clutch per instar] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] represents a moderate reproductive output that is characteristic of intermediate-sized daphniids occupying temperate lakes. These life-history traits, shaped by both predation pressure and food availability, position Daphnia mendotae as a resilient component of its planktonic community.
